newsitem.title: HONG KONG: IPO VIEW - Red chip IPOs to shine in HK's new era.
newsitem.headline: IPO VIEW - Red chip IPOs to shine in HK's new era.

text.p: Initial public offerings (IPO) of "red-chip" companies are expected to be in great demand as Hong Kong begins a new era on its return to China at midnight on Monday.
Analysts said demand for the IPOs of red-chip companies -- Hong Kong-based firms with Chinese financial backing -- remained strong amid hopes for future asset injections.

"The market strength will extend to after the handover. Red chips and their spinoffs will be favourable and companies with a China concept will also be welcomed by the market," said Eugene Law, director at Lippo Securities.
Ample liquidity also would contribute to a healthy market for new offerings, analysts said.
"A high market liquidity will continue enhancing an active and strong market and that will benefit the IPOs," said Percy Au-young, research director at DBS Securities.
Hong Kong reverts to China at midnight (1600 GMT) on June 30 after more than 150 years of British colonial rule.
The Hang Seng Index on Friday ended the last trading day under colonial rule with a record closing high, but red-chip gains were even more impressive.
The China-Affiliated Corporations Index surged 224.63 points, or 6.92 percent, to 3,469.32 while the blue-chip Hang Seng Index gained 68.77 points, or 0.45 percent, to 15,196.79.
"Red chips appear to be more exciting and will continue to be the market focus," said Alex Tang, research director at Yamaichi International.
Analysts predicted scant activity in the IPO market in early July, with business giving way to handover celebrations. The Hong Kong market is closed Monday through Wednesday for handover observances.
Among red chips, China Aerospace International was expected to spin off its telecoms equipment-making unit later in July or in early August, market sources said.

Tianjin municipal government-backed conglomerate Tianjin Industrial was expected to kick off its float in the next three months, while Min Xin Holdings Ltd was seen spinning off its Xiamen International Bank later in the year, they said.
China Telecom (Hong Kong), a telecommuncations operator controlled by China's Ministry of Posts and Telecommunications, was expected to seek a listing in the fourth quarter of 1997.

The recent trend of weak trading debuts for H-shares -- China-incorporated enterprises listed in Hong Kong -- was expected to continue as a large number of H-shares vied for investor funds, analysts said.
The listless response to H-shares was expected to fuel more demand for red chips, they said.
Lennon Chan, executive director at Tai Fook Securities, said that more than 10 H-share companies were expected to come to the market in the near-term.
"Too many H-shares in the market, particularly in infrastructure, will divert investors' interests and people will tend to be more selective," Yamaichi's Tang said.
China Southern Airlines was likely to be the first H-share to come on to the market after the handover, sources said.
The carrier was expected to issue about 1.3 billion H-shares in a dual listing in Hong Kong and New York.
Greater Beijing Region Expressway and China National Aviation Corp (CNAC) were also expected to seek a listing later.
A total of 39 companies listed in the first half of 1997, raising about HK$28.65 billion. Of these, nine were H-shares and five were red-chips or red-chip spinoffs.
Forty-eight firms, including six H-shares and four red-chips, listed in 1996, raising about HK$31.22 billion.
Michael Ng, analyst at ASG Capital, said that the second half of 1997 may see as many new listings as the first half of the year.
Among local IPOs, property group Winsan China (Investments) Ltd was expected to raise HK$600 million in a flotation later in July or in early August, sources said.
Communications services provider City Telecom was also expected to kick off its IPO by the end of July, they said.
